package_info.package_name: N/A (RepoJacking is a technique, not a specific package)
package_info.package_manager: GitHub (affecting downstream: Go, Swift, Packagist, etc.)
package_info.package_versions: All versions of packages relying on vulnerable GitHub repository namespaces
package_info.why_malicious: RepoJacking enables an adversary to take over a previously legitimate repository namespace after a username rename or deletion, allowing them to serve attacker-controlled (potentially malicious) code to all downstream consumers who rely on the original repository URL. This can poison the software supply chain at scale, leading to widespread compromise of dependent projects and systems.

execution_context.trigger: Repository namespace takeover following a username rename or deletion
execution_context.file_location: GitHub repository namespace (e.g., github.com/username/repo), affecting all files within the hijacked repository including source code, workflows, and manifests
required_permissions: Ability to register a previously used GitHub username
Ability to create a repository with the same name as the original under the reclaimed username
Ability to push code and modify repository content

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Attacker creates a repository with the same name as a previously popular or trusted repository under a reclaimed or re-registered username, then pushes attacker-controlled code (such as backdoored source files, malicious GitHub Actions workflows, or tampered package manager manifests) to the repository. This code is then fetched by downstream users or automated systems referencing the original repository URL.
malicious_snippets.code_language: Varies (can include Go, PHP, Swift, JavaScript, YAML, etc., depending on the original repository's ecosystem)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When a downstream user or automated system fetches or installs code from the hijacked repository URL, the attacker-controlled repository serves malicious code or workflows, resulting in the execution of unauthorized or harmful actions on the consumer's system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Hijacking a previously trusted repository namespace to serve new, attacker-controlled code is a classic supply chain attack vector. The sudden reappearance of a repository under a previously retired or renamed username, especially with drastically changed content, is highly indicative of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior expects repository URLs to remain under the control of the original maintainer or be permanently retired. RepoJacking breaks this trust model by allowing a new, unrelated party to control the namespace and serve arbitrary code to unsuspecting consumers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate repository transfers or username changes may occur, but these are typically accompanied by clear communication and do not involve serving malicious or drastically altered code. Legitimate use does not involve deceiving downstream consumers or introducing harmful payloads.
key_indicators: Repository namespace previously belonged to a popular or widely used project
Recent username rename, deletion, and subsequent re-registration by a different account
Repository content, commit history, or workflows change drastically after takeover
Presence of new or modified files such as .github/workflows/* or package manager manifests containing suspicious automation or payloads
Downstream consumers unexpectedly receive code from a new repository owner

attack_chain.action: Attacker monitors for popular repositories whose owners have renamed or deleted their usernames, leaving the old username available for registration.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker can register the old username, opening the opportunity for namespace takeover.

attack_chain.action: Attacker registers the old username and creates a repository with the same name as the original (now-retired) repository.
attack_chain.leads_to: Repository namespace is now under attacker control, matching the original trusted URL.

attack_chain.action: Attacker pushes malicious code, modified workflows, or tampered manifests to the hijacked repository.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is now served to all consumers using the original repository URL.

attack_chain.action: Downstream users or automated systems (such as package managers, CI/CD pipelines) fetch or install code from the hijacked repository, unknowingly executing attacker-supplied code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential compromise of developer systems, CI/CD pipelines, or production environments through execution of malicious code.

behavioral_signatures: Previously popular or widely used repository namespace is suddenly re-registered by a new or unrelated account
Drastic changes in repository content, commit history, or workflows immediately following a username rename or deletion
New repository owner pushes code or workflows containing suspicious or malicious payloads
Unexpected modifications to .github/workflows/* or package manager manifests in a re-registered repository
file_indicators: New or modified .github/workflows/* files containing automation that downloads, executes, or exfiltrates data
Repository files with obfuscated code, credential stealers, or backdoors not present in the original repository
Tampered package manager manifests (e.g., go.mod, composer.json, Package.swift) with suspicious dependencies or scripts
network_indicators: Downstream systems making outbound requests to attacker-controlled domains or IPs after updating dependencies from the hijacked repository
Unexpected external network connections initiated by code fetched from a previously trusted repository URL
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor for re-registration of previously popular repository namespaces following username renames or deletions, especially for high-profile projects. Alert on drastic changes in repository content, commit history, or workflows in such re-registered repositories. Scan for suspicious or malicious code, workflows, or manifests in newly created repositories with previously retired namespaces. Use dependency management tools to pin dependencies to specific commit hashes or verified repository URLs, and avoid relying solely on username-based URLs. Implement automated checks for changes in repository ownership and content for critical dependencies.
